events.excerpt: In collaboration with @winderica TLDR: we port Tornado Cash to Flock, a post-quantum binary-field SNARK, proving a depth-32 withdrawal over SHA-256 in under 30 ms, and describe a simple recovery protocol, requiring only that wallets derive note secrets from a seed, that lets existing pools survive a discrete log break. Introduction Privacy pools such as Tornado Cash rest on the hardness of the discrete logarithm, through both their Pedersen commitments and their Groth16 proofs. Recent autoresearch efforts, both at lowering quantum resource estimates and at breaking hash functions , suggest that quantum discrete-logarithm circuits with far lower gate counts than the published ones, and yet-undiscovered attacks on the hash functions these pools use, may already exist. Recent progress in binary-field proving systems, ZCash’s deployment of ZIP 2005 in Ironwood, and the leanVM aggregation work all point the same way: privacy pools should now start to transition their stack to battle-tested cryptographic primitives. In this post we demonstrate a working Tornado Cash-like pool built on Flock : a plausibly post-quantum transparent hash based binary-field SNARK. We instantiate its merkle tree and nullifier derivation function with SHA-256. We also describe a simple quantum recoverability
events.headline: Faster, Aggregatable and Quantum Safe Privacy Pools

events.excerpt: Hey Cosmonauts, I’ve been exploring an idea for a privacy-focused Cosmos SDK chain and wanted to bring it here before going too far into implementation. The idea is called VeilRoute — a sovereign Cosmos blockchain that acts as a confidential settlement and asset-routing layer between IBC-connected chains. The problem I’m interested in is relatively simple: Cosmos has interoperability through IBC, but what if applications could route assets through a common privacy layer without publicly exposing every internal transfer, amount, balance, or ownership relationship? I’m not proposing changes to the Cosmos Hub or requesting governance funding. This is an early architectural discussion to get technical feedback from people working on Cosmos SDK, IBC, ZK systems, and interchain security. 1. The idea Imagine a user moving ATOM from Cosmos Hub to Osmosis. Today, the public source and destination transactions are observable, along with the relevant IBC packet information. With VeilRoute, the proposed flow would be: Cosmos Hub / Other IBC Chain | IBC Deposit | v +---------------+ | VeilRoute | | | | Shielded Pool | | ZK Validation | | Private Notes | | Audit Records | +---------------+ | IBC Withdrawal | v Destination IBC Chain Users would deposit an IBC asset, shield it into a private not

events.excerpt: Should the Cosmos Hub have its own price oracle? CosmWasm is now permissionless on the Hub, but there is no price oracle available to contracts. Pyth dropped CosmWasm, SEDA is EVM-only, and Band over IBC is slow and costs fees on every query. Without prices, we can’t build any advanced defi on the Hub. So these apps get built on chains like Injective or dYdX, and ATOM ends up used everywhere except on its own chain. Idea: integrate an enshrined oracle based on the Slinky fork. Validators would publish prices at every block, secured by the Hub’s own validator set, with no dependency on an external provider. And beyond the Hub: these prices could be distributed over IBC to any connected chain that lacks an oracle. The Hub would become an interchain’s price provider, with fees flowing back to ATOM stakers. Longer term: prices are only the first step. The same validator-voted mechanism could later carry other data the interchain needs, such as LST exchange rates, proof of reserves or other verified off-chain data. The Hub would become the interchain’s trusted data layer. The Community Pool could fund the development and audit. Would you support this direction? Validators, would you be willing to run an oracle sidecar? 20 posts - 7 participants Read full topic
events.headline: Oracle on Cosmos Hub

events.excerpt: Release v5.20.0 New Model additions Muse Spark Open Muse Spark Open is a multimodal mixture-of-experts model from Meta that takes text, images, audio, and video as input and generates text. It has 816B total parameters (42B active per token) and a context window of up to 1,048,576 tokens shared across modalities. It is trained for agentic coding tasks such as multi-file editing, debugging, and tool use. Checkpoints are available in BF16 and NVFP4 formats. Links: Documentation | Blog Post Add Muse Spark Open ( #49644 ) by @guarin in #49644 Ling 3.0 Ling 3.0 Flash is a hybrid Mixture-of-Experts language model from InclusionAI. Its decoder groups five Kimi Delta Attention (KDA) layers with one Multi-head Latent Attention (MLA) layer. events.excerpt: At a glance A new form of computing . Zero-knowledge proofs let you run a workload and receive, alongside the result, a short proof that the program ran correctly. Anyone can check the proof in milliseconds, without rerunning the program, without trusting whoever ran it, and without needing data on which the program was run. Three grand challenges have stood in the way of broad adoption : making proofs fast enough to produce, making them available to normal programs without cryptographic expertise, and resting them on cryptography that will still be trusted many decades from now. Magnetar makes major progress on all three challenges. It proves programs written in Rust, Go, or C, runs 10 to 39 times faster on average than the prior fastest comparable systems, and rests its security only on standard hash functions. It is the latest result of more than a decade of research at Microsoft Research on making zero-knowledge proofs practical. A new form of computing Every result a computer produces comes with an implicit question: did the program run as claimed and produce correct outputs? Today, answering that question often requires a degree of trust alongside verification. We trust the operator, the vendor, the counterparty, or the agent, and we rely on contracts, audits, and logs to e

events.excerpt: v2.10.3 is a security and stability release on top of v2.10.2 . It's the public release of v2.10.3-priv , which most validators and major RPC providers already run. No hardfork, no database schema change, no resync required. Nodes can be upgraded one at a time, in any order. Highlights Execution : parallel (BlockSTM V2) balance reads are resolved correctly across a self-destruct boundary ( #2403 ). Shared block caches are size-capped and per-tx code hashes memoized, which lowers importer memory under heavy keccak / ecrecover load. Log counting while tracing no longer copies logs ( #2460 ). Txpool : pending chains stranded behind a head that can't be mined are evicted after txpool.strandedlifetime . Filtered addresses also apply to SetCode (type 4) authorizations. The pool signer is no longer swapped when allow-unprotected-txs is set ( #2464 ). Storage trie preload : segmented BFS queue for the preload, plus optional address-cache persistence across restarts. On a mainnet sentry, preload on restart drops from about 1h25m to about 4s. P2P : static peers stay dialed across jails and full dynamic slots ( #2438 ), and are kept out of the peer dropper. RPC : the execution slot is re-acquired between batch items, and the RPC execution pool request timeout from config is applied. Heimdal

events.excerpt: Microsoft today issued updates to fix more than 1,400 security vulnerabilities in its Windows operating systems and other software. Today’s epic patch batch dwarfs September’s record of nearly 1,000 fixes, which was already about ten times the normal monthly patch load from Redmond. Just one of the weaknesses patched this week is considered a “zero day,” or already exploited in the wild. CVE-2026-96951 is a security feature bypass in the Windows Shell that affects Windows 10 and 11 systems, as well as some Server versions. Windows 10 users might be wondering if they can still expect security updates after this month. Microsoft had been slated to stop shipping updates for Windows 10 systems in October 2025, but ended up adding another year of free updates after considerable pushback. A few months ago, Microsoft quietly extended that support for another year (until October 2027). At least 78 of the flaws fixed this month are rated “critical,” meaning they could be exploited with little or no action by the user, and most of those critical bugs allow an attacker to execute code of their choice on the vulnerable system.
